name: Part 1 — Practice
tagline: The full Quarter 3 question bank, with the language to answer it
blurb: Forty-four topic frames from the 2026 Quarter 3 forecast, the everyday vocabulary each one needs, the grammar that Part 1 answers actually run on, and three model answers to compare against — after you have recorded your own.
modelQ: Are street markets common in your country?
modelType: The your country type — hedged generalisation, split the population, place yourself.

items: a stone's throw from
phrase
/stəʊnz θrəʊ/
Very close by. Slightly informal, and much more vivid than near.
I'm lucky, really — the market is a stone's throw from my building, so I never plan my shopping.
built up
adjective
/bɪlt ˈʌp/
Densely covered with buildings. Usually carries mild regret.
The whole area has got far more built up since I moved in — there was a field there five years ago.
run-down
adjective
/rʌn ˈdaʊn/
In poor repair. Precise where old is vague.
It's a bit run-down, to be honest, but the rent is half what you'd pay two streets over.
within walking distance
phrase
/ˈwɔːkɪŋ ˈdɪstəns/
Close enough to walk. The standard answer to any convenience question.
Almost everything I need is within walking distance, which is the main reason I've stayed.
settle in
phrasal verb
/ˈsetl ɪn/
Become comfortable somewhere new. Takes time as an object.
It took me a good six months to settle in — I didn't know a single neighbour at first.
put up with
phrasal verb
/pʊt ʌp wɪð/
Tolerate something unpleasant. Implies you had no choice.
The one thing I can't put up with is the construction noise; it starts at six every morning.
have a sweet tooth
idiom
/swiːt tuːθ/
Like sugary food. Almost always said about yourself, humorously.
I've got a terrible sweet tooth, so dessert is usually the part of the meal I'm there for.
can't stand
phrase
/kɑːnt stænd/
Strongly dislike. Far more natural in speech than I hate.
I can't stand coriander — my whole family finds this hilarious because it's in everything here.
a rip-off
noun
/ə ˈrɪp ɒf/
Something badly overpriced. Informal and a little indignant.
The coffee near my office is an absolute rip-off, so I make my own and feel smug about it.
browse
verb
/braʊz/
Look without intending to buy.
Half the time I'm just browsing — I'll spend an hour in a bookshop and come out with nothing.
worth every penny
idiom
/wɜːθ ˈevri ˈpeni/
Expensive but justified by use.
My headphones cost more than I'd like to admit, but they've been worth every penny.
splash out on
phrasal verb
/splæʃ ˈaʊt/
Spend more than usual, willingly and occasionally.
Once or twice a year I'll splash out on a proper meal somewhere, and the rest of the time I cook.
scroll through
phrasal verb
/skrəʊl θruː/
Move through content on a screen, usually without purpose.
I'll scroll through my phone for twenty minutes and genuinely not remember a single thing I saw.
a time sink
noun
/taɪm sɪŋk/
Something that consumes far more time than it deserves.
Short videos are a complete time sink — you open one and lose an evening.
keep up with
phrasal verb
/kiːp ˈʌp wɪð/
Stay informed about people or events.
I mostly use it to keep up with cousins abroad; otherwise we'd never speak at all.
binge-watch
verb
/bɪndʒ wɒtʃ/
Watch many episodes in one sitting. Informal, recent.
I binge-watched an entire Korean series over one weekend and regretted it on Monday.
glance at
verb
/ɡlɑːns æt/
Look at briefly. Precise where check is vague.
I only glance at the news in the morning — anything longer and I'd never leave the house.
on the go
idiom
/ɒn ðə ˈɡəʊ/
While travelling or busy.
I do almost all my listening on the go, usually on the bus, rarely sitting down.
a creature of habit
idiom
/ˈkriːtʃər əv ˈhæbɪt/
Someone who likes the same routine. Ideal for morning-routine questions.
I'm a complete creature of habit — same breakfast, same route, same seat on the bus.
drag myself out of bed
phrase
/dræɡ maɪˈself/
Get up with great difficulty.
On winter mornings I have to drag myself out of bed, and the first hour is a write-off.
run on empty
idiom
/rʌn ɒn ˈempti/
Keep going while exhausted.
By Friday afternoon I'm running on empty and I've stopped being useful to anyone.
nod off
phrasal verb
/nɒd ˈɒf/
Fall asleep accidentally.
I nodded off on the bus last week and went four stops past my own.
unwind
verb
/ʌnˈwaɪnd/
Relax after effort. More sophisticated than relax.
I need about half an hour to unwind before I can concentrate on anything in the evening.
shattered
adjective
/ˈʃætəd/
Extremely tired. British, informal, stronger than tired.
I was absolutely shattered after the trip and slept eleven hours without moving.
get on well with
phrasal verb
/ɡet ɒn ˈwel/
Have a good relationship with someone.
I get on well with most of my neighbours, though I couldn't tell you half their names.
easy-going
adjective
/ˈiːzi ˈɡəʊɪŋ/
Relaxed and tolerant. Warm, informal.
She's incredibly easy-going, which is probably why people tell her things they shouldn't.
bring somebody up
phrasal verb
/brɪŋ ʌp/
Raise a child. Usually in the passive when about yourself.
I was brought up to greet people properly, and I still feel guilty if I forget.
make small talk
collocation
/smɔːl tɔːk/
Chat about unimportant things. Central to politeness topics.
I'm hopeless at making small talk with strangers — I run out of things to say in about forty seconds.
have a laugh
phrase
/hæv ə lɑːf/
Enjoy yourself with others. British and informal.
We don't do anything special, we just have a laugh and complain about work.
look up to
phrasal verb
/lʊk ʌp tə/
Admire and respect, usually someone older.
I've always looked up to my aunt — she went back to university at forty-five.
keep my brain ticking over
idiom
/ˈtɪkɪŋ ˈəʊvə/
Stay mentally active. Gently self-deprecating.
I do a crossword most evenings, mainly to keep my brain ticking over.
it slipped my mind
idiom
/slɪpt maɪ ˈmaɪnd/
I forgot. Softer and more natural than I forgot.
I was supposed to call her back and it completely slipped my mind until the next day.
a memory like a sieve
idiom
/sɪv/
Forget things constantly. Said about yourself, humorously.
I've got a memory like a sieve for names — faces I never forget, names I lose instantly.
get to grips with
phrasal verb
/ɡet tə ˈɡrɪps/
Begin to understand something difficult.
It took me most of a term to get to grips with statistics, and I'm still not confident.
hands-on
adjective
/hændz ˈɒn/
Practical rather than theoretical.
I learn best in a hands-on way — reading about something never sticks for me.
fall behind
phrasal verb
/fɔːl bɪˈhaɪnd/
Fail to keep pace with others.
I fell behind badly in my first year and spent the summer catching up.

grammar.intro: Part 1 answers are short, so the grammar is visible. These five structures cover almost every question type in the forecast, and the six error patterns below are the ones that recur most in Vietnamese learners' speech — each one costs marks under Grammatical Range and Accuracy even when the meaning is perfectly clear.

structures.n: Present simple with adverbs of frequency
structures.ex: I hardly ever go. / I'm hardly ever at home before eight.
structures.note: Frequency adverbs go before the main verb but after be. Getting this wrong is the single most audible Part 1 grammar slip.

structures.form: used to + bare infinitive  ·  would + bare infinitive (repeated actions only)
structures.ex: I used to live nearer the park, and we would walk there every Sunday.
structures.note: Used to works for states and actions; would only for repeated actions. I would live there is wrong for a past state.

structures.use: Hypothetical questions: Would you like to…? Would you ever…?
structures.form: If + past simple, would + bare infinitive
structures.ex: If it were a shorter trip, I might reconsider.
structures.note: Free marks. The question hands you the modal; matching it is the easiest range you will earn all test.

structures.form: far / a good deal / nothing like as … as
structures.ex: It's nothing like as crowded as it used to be. / Online is far quicker.
structures.note: A bare comparative is Band 6. A qualified comparative is Band 7 and takes one extra word.

structures.use: How long have you…? and any change-over-time question.
structures.form: have/has + past participle, often with for / since / lately
structures.ex: The area has got much busier over the last few years.
structures.note: Vietnamese has no direct equivalent, so this is systematically under-used. Deploying it once per Part 1 is worth doing deliberately.

errors.bad: I like <s>the</s> street markets because they sell <s>a</s> fresh food.
errors.good: I like street markets because they sell fresh food.
errors.why: Plural and uncountable nouns used in a general sense take no article. This is the highest-frequency error in the whole test and examiners register it as a persistent basic error, which caps Grammatical Range at Band 7.

errors.bad: He gave me many useful <s>advices</s> and <s>informations</s>.
errors.good: He gave me a lot of useful advice and information.
errors.why: Advice, information, furniture, equipment, homework, news, research are uncountable in English. Add a piece of if you need to count them.

errors.bad: My brother <s>go</s> to the gym every day and he never <s>miss</s> a session.
errors.good: My brother goes to the gym every day and he never misses a session.
errors.why: Almost every candidate knows this rule and a great many drop it while speaking. It is not a knowledge gap; it is an automaticity gap, and only speaking practice closes it.

errors.bad: I <s>very like</s> it. / I like it <s>very</s>.
errors.good: I like it very much. / I really like it.
errors.why: Very modifies adjectives and adverbs, not verbs. With a verb, use very much after the object, or really before the verb.

errors.bad: It <s>depends of</s> the weather. / I'm <s>interested about</s> history. / We <s>discussed about</s> it.
errors.good: It depends on the weather. / I'm interested in history. / We discussed it.
errors.why: These three are the most frequent preposition errors in Vietnamese learners' English. Discuss takes no preposition at all.

errors.bad: <s>Although</s> I live near the park, <s>but</s> I hardly ever go.
errors.good: Although I live near the park, I hardly ever go.
errors.why: English uses one conjunction per relationship. The doubling comes directly from Vietnamese sentence structure and is instantly recognisable to an examiner.

models.html: Yes, street markets are very common in my country. In Vietnam, almost every area has a market and people go there every morning to buy food. It is cheaper than supermarket and also the vegetables are more fresh. My mother always goes to the market near my house.

notes.fc: The answer is clear and on topic, with simple connectives (and, also). There is no hesitation, but there is also no shaping — the ideas arrive in the order they occurred.
notes.lr: Entirely high-frequency: very common, cheaper, fresh. Meaning is never in doubt, which is exactly what Band 6 describes: enough resource to discuss the topic, with limited flexibility.
notes.gr: Two errors visible. Than supermarket is missing an article; more fresh should be fresher. Neither obscures meaning, which is the Band 6 condition, but both are basic and both recur.
notes.pr: Intelligible, with content-word stress present but not sustained. Rhythm is even across the whole answer.

models.html: Very much so, though it rather depends where you are. In smaller towns they're still where most people do their food shopping — my grandmother has been going to the same one for about thirty years. In the cities, though, the younger crowd has drifted towards supermarkets, mainly because you can get everything under one roof and nobody expects you to haggle. I'm somewhere in between, honestly — market for vegetables, supermarket for everything else.

notes.fc: The answer has a visible shape: hedged generalisation, then a split by place, then the speaker's own position. Markers vary in function (though, mainly because, honestly) rather than repeating, which is the Band 7 requirement.
notes.lr: Drifted towards, the younger crowd, under one roof, haggle. Less common items appear naturally and the register stays conversational. There is an awareness of style that Band 6 lacks.
notes.gr: Present perfect continuous (has been going), present perfect (has drifted), a causal subordinate clause and an elliptical final clause. Error-free throughout, though the range is not yet fully free.
notes.pr: Contrastive stress on smaller towns against the cities makes the structure audible before the words do. The final clause drops into a lower, faster register, which is a genuine phonological choice.

models.html:
Still very common, though I'd say they're quietly changing function. Twenty years ago a street market was simply where food came from; now, in Hanoi at least, it's increasingly something you go to instead of a supermarket for reasons that aren't really about price. Freshness, partly. Knowing the person who sold you the fish, mostly.

My grandmother has bought from the same stall since before I was born and would sooner go hungry than buy fish from a chiller cabinet — which tells you it was never a transaction to begin with. So yes, common — but I suspect what's keeping them alive now isn't economics.

notes.fc: The answer reframes the question — from are they common to why are they still common — and resolves on that reframing. The two paragraphs are structurally distinct and the closing clause answers the original question and the reframed one simultaneously. No hesitation to find language.
notes.lr: Quietly changing function, chiller cabinet, a transaction to begin with, keeping them alive. Idiomatic, precise, and capable of understatement. The two-word sentences carry as much lexical weight as the long ones.
notes.gr: Would sooner … than, a non-defining relative clause commenting on the whole preceding clause, since with present perfect, and a fronted concessive. Structures change with rhetorical purpose and the majority are error-free.
notes.pr: Freshness, partly. Knowing the person who sold you the fish, mostly. — two fragments delivered at different speeds, with the second slower. The falling contour on mostly does the argumentative work. This is stress and intonation conveying precise meaning, which is the Band 8 descriptor verbatim.
